Monsoon to withdraw from MP by October 10:Bright sunshine for 3 days, then rain; expert says days will remain hot
Bhopal will see bright sunshine over the next three days.
The southwest monsoon will withdraw from Madhya Pradesh by 10 October. Until then, the state will experience intense sunshine and rain. The sun will shine across the entire state, including Bhopal, Indore, Ujjain, Gwalior and Jabalpur, over the next three days, while rain is expected in the eastern parts on the fourth day, 5 October. Weather expert Shailendra Kumar Nayak said there would be heat during the day and cool conditions at night.
The monsoon period ended on 30 September, but it has not yet withdrawn from any district. According to IMD (the Meteorological Centre) Bhopal, the monsoon withdrawal line is passing through Punjab, Haryana, Delhi and Rajasthan. In Madhya Pradesh, it is currently situated over the Gwalior-Chambal and Ujjain divisions.
Therefore, the monsoon is likely to begin withdrawing from here. It will then withdraw from the Indore, Bhopal, Narmadapuram, Sagar, Jabalpur, Rewa and Shahdol divisions. The process could begin on Friday or Saturday, and the monsoon may withdraw from the entire state by 10 October.
October is a month of transition
According to the India Meteorological Department, October in the state has traditionally brought rain, heat and cold. The same pattern is expected this year as well. October is also a changeover period, as the monsoon begins to withdraw during the month. This leads to clear skies, resulting in heat during the day and cooler temperatures at night. A drop in night temperatures was recorded in several cities on the very first day.
Less rain, but the heat may be more noticeable
Weather expert Nayak said maximum temperatures are likely to remain above normal in most parts of the state in October. Light rain is also expected in some places. Light rain may occur in Panna, Satna, Rewa, Mauganj, Maihar, Sidhi, Singrauli, Shahdol and Anuppur on 5 October.
State Records 35.8 Inches of Rain This Season During the southwest monsoon, the state received a total of 908.4 mm, or 35.8 inches, of rain-95.9 per cent of the normal rainfall. This is 1.5 inches less than the normal 37.3 inches (949.5 mm). Overall, rainfall was 4 per cent below normal. The eastern parts received 4 per cent more rain, while the western parts received 12 per cent less than average.
Eastern Parts of the State-The figure is 4 per cent above normal in the Jabalpur, Rewa, Sagar and Shahdol divisions. Most districts have received more rain than their quota, but Balaghat, Chhindwara, Damoh, Jabalpur, Narsinghpur, Pandhurna, Rewa, Sagar and Seoni received 5 per cent to 21 per cent less rainfall.
Western Parts of the State-Alirajpur, Ashoknagar, Barwani, Betul, Dewas, Dhar, Harda, Indore, Jhabua, Khandwa, Mandsaur, Morena, Narmadapuram, Neemuch, Raisen, Ratlam, Sehore, Shajapur, Ujjain and Vidisha received 9 per cent to 51 per cent less rain than average.
Rainfall quota complete in these 25 districts
Bhopal, Rajgarh, Burhanpur, Khargone, Katni, Mandla, Dindori, Gwalior, Guna, Datia, Panna, Chhatarpur, Tikamgarh, Niwari, Maihar, Agar-Malwa, Bhind, Sheopur, Singrauli, Sidhi, Satna, Mauganj, Shahdol, Umaria and Anuppur have received their full rainfall quota.
June was dry this time, resulting in a lower figure
According to the Meteorological Department, rainfall in June was 14 per cent below normal. The figure rose after heavy rain in the early days of July. The monsoon then went into a break twice, and there was no rain for several days.
A strong system became active again in the final week. Despite this, the state received 13 per cent less rainfall. The rainfall quota for July, August and September was met in full, but the deficit in June could not be made up. This is why the state has received 4 per cent less rainfall this year.
The state's normal rainfall is 37.3 inches
The state's normal rainfall is 37.3 inches. The normal rainfall in Bhopal, Indore, Jabalpur and Gwalior districts is between 38 and 39 inches.
Now find out when and what the weather was like in October in five major cities...
Bhopal: Temperature hit a record 38 degrees Celsius in 2012 Bhopal's normal average maximum and minimum temperatures in October are 32.7 and 19.1 degrees Celsius (°C), respectively. Over the past 10 years, the temperature has remained above 32°C. It reached 36.4°C in 2017. In 2012, the mercury hit a record 38°C.
The minimum temperature was 11.7°C on 12 October 2012. October also has a history of rainfall. In 1955, 7.5 inches of rain fell throughout the month. A record 5 inches of rain fell in 24 hours on 6 October 2009. Last year, 3.2 inches of rain was recorded throughout the month.
Indore: Minimum temperature recorded at 6.2°C 25 years ago
All three seasons can be experienced in Indore. Looking at the past 10 years, from 2016 to 2025, the daytime temperature has reached 35°C on three occasions. The night-time temperature remains between 14 and 16°C. The effect of the cold intensifies at night during the last week of October. Indore has a trend of receiving rain this month. The highest rainfall, 4 inches, was recorded in 2013. One inch of rain was recorded last year.
Indore's daytime temperature reached 37.8°C on 22 October 2000. This remains the record. Twenty-five years ago, the night-time temperature recorded on 22 October 1999 was 6.2°C. It was the coldest night on record. More than 9 inches of rain was recorded in October 1985. The highest 24-hour rainfall, 6.19 inches, was recorded on 9 October 1985. Last year, 5.1 inches of rain was recorded over the entire month.
Gwalior: Daytime temperatures rise above 38°C
Gwalior experiences intense heat during the day even in October. In 2015, the maximum temperature reached 39°C. Over the past 10 years, temperatures have generally remained above 35°C. On 27 October 1994, the daytime temperature was recorded at 40.1°C, the highest ever recorded so far. The average maximum temperature here is 34.2°C and the average minimum temperature is 19.3°C.
Just as intense as the heat is here, the cold is equally pronounced. The temperature was recorded at 11.9°C in 2018. The minimum temperature was 8.9°C on 31 October 1952. Eight out of 10 years also saw periods of rain. Rainfall of 5 inches was recorded in 2022 and 4.4 inches in 2024. The highest monthly rainfall was recorded in 1956, at 8.68 inches. The heaviest rainfall in 24 hours occurred on 13 October 1955, when 6 inches of rain fell.
Jabalpur: The coldest night was recorded 74 years ago
In Jabalpur, the average maximum temperature in October is 31.8°C, while the average minimum temperature is 20.3°C. However, over the past 10 years, both daytime and night-time temperatures have remained higher than these averages. The maximum temperature recorded on 5 October 1966 was 37.9°C, the highest so far. The minimum temperature on 30 October 1952 was 10.5°C.
The highest monthly rainfall was recorded in 1916, at 10.46 inches. The highest 24-hour rainfall, measuring 5 inches, was recorded on 4 October 1977. Last year too, the city received 7 inches of rain throughout the month.
Ujjain: Rainfall absent in two of the past 10 years
Ujjain did not receive any rainfall in October in two of the past 10 years. The highest monthly rainfall was recorded in 2009, at 4.46 inches. The highest rainfall in 24 hours was recorded on 5 October 2009. The city received 92 mm, or 3.62 inches, of rain that day.
On the other hand, the daytime temperature was recorded at 39°C on 5 October 2002, the highest ever recorded. The minimum temperature was 8.1°C on 29 October 1983.

A major, highly unusual, and exceptionally long-lasting October heat wave
Driven by a strong high-pressure system building over the eastern Pacific and the West Coast, this multi-week setup will deliver dangerously hot temperatures well above normal
Good Thursday evening, Central Coast from Meteorologist Jim Castillo
Dangerous and Long-Lasting Heat Wave Heading for San Luis Obispo and Santa Barbara Counties
A major, highly unusual, and exceptionally long-lasting October heat wave is set to impact San Luis Obispo County and Santa Barbara County, beginning Friday and persisting through all of next week, with potential extensions into the second week of October. Driven by a strong high-pressure system building over the eastern Pacific and the West Coast, this multi-week setup will deliver dangerously hot temperatures well above normal.
Key Meteorological Drivers
Pressure gradients are weakening, shifting to offshore
While this is an offshore flow pattern, it is not a traditional because upper-level support lacks persistent gusty winds. Expect only brief, sub-advisory north-to-northeast breezes.
This extreme heat will reach right down to the coastal zones of Santa Barbara County with an Extreme Heat Warning Friday through next Thursday
Regional Timeline and Temperature Breakdown
San Luis Obispo and Northern Santa Barbara Counties: Warming is delayed slightly by a day, ramping up significantly over the weekend. Highs away from the beaches will climb, with the interior valleys soaring into the lower 100s. Heat advisories are officially in effect from Saturday morning through Sunday evening in San Luis Obispo County.
Santa Barbara County Interior, Valleys, and Mountain Zones (Including the Santa Ynez Valley, Santa Lucia Mountains, Santa Ynez Mountains, and Los Padres National Forest sections): Expect extreme interior maximums, with local hot spots reaching over 100 degrees.
Coastal Communities: Even the beaches and coastal plains of Santa Barbara County will experience significant heat, with daytime highs pushing into the 80s and some 90s.
Long-Term Outlook (Monday through Thursday and Beyond)
The heat will not relent easily. Monday and Tuesday will mirror the weekend conditions closely. Looking toward the middle of next week (Wednesday through Friday), computer models indicate potential supplemental upper-level northeast wind support, which could drive temperatures even higher and threaten daily records. Early indications point to potential relief by next weekend, but until then, residents across San Luis Obispo and Santa Barbara counties should prepare for relentless heat.

Reading Time: 2 minutesThe National Weather Service has issued an Extreme Heat Warning for portions of San Diego County starting Friday morning. The combination of extreme heat and Santa Ana winds in the forecast is prompting the possibility of power shutoffs for some SDG&E customers through Oct. 5.
The County of San Diego urges residents to prepare for potential power outages and take steps to prevent heat-related illnesses as temperatures climb.
Forecasters expect dangerously high temperatures through next Thursday, with highs in the 90s near the coast and reaching the 100s in inland valleys. Warm overnight lows will make it harder for people to cool down, and the hot, dry weather will raise wildfire danger across the region.
Hot, dry and windy conditions often overlap with Red Flag periods, increasing the chance of fast‑moving wildfires. SDG&E is monitoring conditions and may activate Public Safety Power Shutoffs (PSPS) if wildfire risk increases. The PSPS Dashboard provides real‑time information on potentially impacted communities, and the utility will post additional written updates as conditions change.
The County urges residents to stay alert to fire‑weather advisories, avoid activities that can spark fires, secure trailer chains, dispose of cigarettes safely and keep household emergency go‑kits ready. These prevention steps reduce the risk of ignition and support community safety.
Stay Safe During the Heat
Stay informed by signing up for emergency alerts at AlertSanDiego.org, where you can register your phone number, receive important notifications and find preparedness information.
When temperatures rise this high, heat can be dangerous for people and pets. Extreme heat can cause heat exhaustion or heatstroke, especially for older adults, children, people with chronic conditions, pregnant individuals and outdoor workers.
Signs of heat illness include dizziness, nausea, confusion, heavy sweating, headaches or fainting. Seek help immediately if symptoms appear.
Residents should take basic steps to stay safe:
- Stay in air‑conditioned spaces during peak heat.
- Drink plenty of water and avoid sugary or alcoholic drinks.
- Wear lightweight, loose‑fitting clothing.
- Avoid using fans alone when temperatures exceed 90 degrees.
- Never leave children, older adults or pets in vehicles.
The County’s Cool Zones, including 33 branch libraries and community centers, offer air‑conditioned spaces where people can escape the heat. The County’s website lists all Cool Zone locations and includes an interactive map.
Tijuana River Valley Effects
Near the Tijuana River Valley, the County monitors hydrogen sulfide odors, which increase during heat events. The County advises residents to limit outdoor activity, close windows and run air‑conditioning on recirculate to reduce exposure.
People can get more information at the County’s Tijuana River Valley Environmental Dashboard.
Remember Your Pets
Pets need protection from extreme heat. The County urges owners to keep animals indoors when possible, provide continuous clean water, limit outdoor activity to early morning or evening and never leave pets in parked cars.
County Encourages Power‑Outage Readiness
With possible Public Safety Power Shutoffs approaching, the County advises residents to:
- Visit Cool Zones if indoor temperatures rise to unsafe levels.
- Prepare communication plans with family and neighbors.
- Keep water on hand and monitor official alerts.
County emergency teams continue tracking weather and fire conditions and coordinating with public‑safety partners to safeguard the community throughout the heat event. County departments are also reaching out to vulnerable people they serve in areas that may be most impacted.

A prolonged heat wave is hitting Long Beach. It will feel even hotter because of El Niño
Learn more about what El Niño means for Long Beach and how you can be prepared at LBPost.com/elnino. Support useful, community-centered reporting like this with a donation.
An unusually persistent heat wave will arrive in Long Beach — and the rest of the region — this weekend, with high humidity and near triple-digit temperatures on some days. Most of the city will see highs in the 90s from Friday through Thursday, with the hottest weather expected Saturday.
Max temperatures will be roughly 15-20 degrees hotter than normal for this time of year, according to the National Weather Service.
It’s going to feel extra hot because of increased humidity from Hurricane Rachel, currently off the coast of Mexico. That humidity is expected to arrive on Monday and remain through at least Wednesday, forecasters said, and overnight lows will remain elevated — in the mid-70s through Wednesday as well.
The El Niño weather pattern, brought on by warmer ocean temperatures, is directly related to the higher overnight temperatures and elevated humidity, said Daniel Swain, a climate scientist.
“This [heat wave] won’t be as humid as August, but it also won’t be as dry as it would normally be,” Swain said. “So you’re still going to feel that added oomph.”
Although the humidity won’t be as bad as heat waves over the past two months, forecasters warn that its prolonged nature could be dangerous.
“The relentless heat will have a hazardous wearing down effect on people, especially the very young and old,” forecasters said.
An extreme heat watch will be in effect from Friday morning through Thursday, with forecasters warning that the risk of heat-related illnesses will be high.
Residents are advised to drink plenty of fluids, stay in an air-conditioned room, avoid the sun when possible and check up on relatives and neighbors.
How to Cool Off
Free air conditioning is available at cooling centers throughout the city, including all public libraries. You can find a full list of locations and when they’re open here.
Long Beach also has aquatic playgrounds set up at Alamitos Beach (between Fifth and Sixth places) and at Bay Shore Beach. Those are open daily from 10 a.m. to 7 p.m., but all participants must pass a swim test.
Public pools are available at Martin Luther King Jr. Park (1910 Lemon Ave.) and Silverado Park (1540 W. 32nd St.). Children age 17 and under can swim for free, while the entry fee is $3 for adults and $2 for seniors — defined as anyone age 50 and older.
by
Jacob Sisneros and John Donegan
Cooler temperatures should start to arrive on Oct. 10.

15:00, 2 October 2026
Metro movement through the Southern Bridge during the yellow alert level is ready to be restored after expert conclusions.
Kyiv Metro is ready to restore train movement through the Southern Bridge during the yellow air raid alert level after receiving an expert assessment of the structure’s condition. This was reported by the Mayor of Kyiv, Vitaliy Klytschko.
According to him, the issue of the green metro line movement was discussed at a meeting of the Capital Defense Council. The metro is ready to return to this mode of operation after scientific institutes provide an assessment of the Southern Bridge’s condition. The Ministry of Communities and Territories Development of Ukraine has sent a corresponding request to them.
The Defense Council also considered the issue of transport movement across the bridges over the Dnipro River. The meeting was attended by military personnel, law enforcement officers, representatives of the State Emergency Service, and communal services. They provided proposals to ensure safety while considering the necessity of transport connection between the left and right banks of the capital.
The proposals of the Kyiv Defense Council will be forwarded to central government authorities.
